content: Ebola virus disease (EVD) is classified as one of the viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs). It is a severe and often fatal illness that affects both humans and nonhuman primates. The virus is transmitted through direct contact with the blood or bodily fluids (such as urine, saliva, feces, vomit, and semen) of an infected individual or through exposure to objects contaminated with infected blood or bodily fluids. The incubation period typically ranges from 8 to 10 days, though it can vary from 2 to 21 days in rare cases. Patients become infectious once symptoms appear and remain so during the later stages of the disease and even postmortem. Since its discovery, Ebola has been responsible for several significant and highly publicized outbreaks. The Ebola virus was named after the Ebola River Valley in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (formerly Zaire), near the site of a 1976 outbreak at a mission run by Flemish nuns. Since its initial identification, five subtypes of the virus have been recognized: Zaire, Sudan, Reston, Tai Forest (Ivory Coast), and Bundibugyo, each named after the location of its discovery. The Ebola virus primarily infects cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system but also targets hepatocytes, spongiocytes, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells. This leads to tissue necrosis and disruption of hematological and coagulation systems. Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected individuals or animals. The natural reservoir of the virus remains unidentified. Ebola infection is caused by a virus belonging to the Filoviridae family. Three subtypes—Ebola-Zaire, Ebola-Sudan, and Ebola-Ivory Coast—are known to cause disease in humans. Human cases have been largely confined to parts of Africa. A small number of individuals in the United States were infected with the Reston subtype, but they did not develop symptoms of the disease. Ebola must be differentiated from other diseases that cause hemorrhage and/or high fever, such as Marburg virus, Lassa fever, typhoid fever, and malaria. Clinicians must first rule out more common causes of fever before considering VHFs like Ebola. The suspicion of a VHF should be based on epidemiological and demographic factors, as well as clinical signs and symptoms. Ebola should be suspected in febrile individuals who, within three weeks prior to symptom onset, have either: 1) traveled to an area where VHFs have recently occurred; 2) had direct unprotected contact with blood, bodily fluids, secretions, or excretions of a person or animal with VHF; 3) been in contact with someone who was ill with fever and bleeding or who died from an unexplained febrile illness with bleeding; 4) worked in a laboratory handling hemorrhagic fever viruses; 5) experienced persistent fever after three days of empiric treatment, especially if accompanied by bleeding or shock; or 6) presented with no other identifiable cause for their symptoms. Ebola outbreaks have been largely restricted to Africa. Governments and individuals should act swiftly to quarantine affected areas. The lack of roads and transportation in remote regions often helps contain outbreaks. The potential for widespread epidemics is considered low due to the high case-fatality rate, the rapid progression of the disease, and the remote locations where infections typically occur. The primary risk factors for Ebola virus disease include travel to endemic areas, healthcare professionals caring for infected patients, and researchers working with animal models of the disease. Ebola infection progresses rapidly and is often fatal without supportive care. Complications include multiorgan failure and shock. The prognosis is poor and depends on the specific strain of the virus. The Zaire strain has a mortality rate as high as 90%. Ebola presents with a range of symptoms, including fever, chills, vomiting, diarrhea, generalized pain or malaise, and sometimes internal and external bleeding. These symptoms follow an incubation period of 2 to 21 days. While all Ebola virus species cause similar symptoms, the severity may vary between species. On physical examination, Ebola is commonly associated with the acute onset of high fever, chills, hemorrhage, swollen joints, weakness, rash, and conjunctival injection (red eyes). Laboratory findings in Ebola infection are nonspecific and may include abnormalities in white blood cell counts, blood chemistry tests, and liver function tests. These changes can contribute to clotting disruptions and bleeding. While clinical findings may raise suspicion for Ebola, definitive diagnosis requires laboratory confirmation. Diagnostic tests include antigen-capture enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), IgM ELISA, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and virus isolation, which can detect the virus within days of symptom onset. Later in the disease course or after recovery, IgM and IgG antibodies can be tested. In deceased patients, diagnosis can be confirmed using immunohistochemistry, virus isolation, or PCR. Treatment for Ebola is primarily supportive and includes maintaining fluid and electrolyte balance, homeostasis, adequate oxygenation, and blood pressure, as well as managing any secondary infections. All patients with confirmed or suspected VHFs should be isolated with appropriate contact precautions. Currently, no vaccine is available. Preventing Ebola transmission involves implementing measures such as isolating infected patients, using personal protective equipment (PPE) like gloves, masks, and gowns, practicing routine hand hygiene, safely handling and disposing of sharp objects, proper waste management, and careful handling of human remains after death. Although no effective human vaccine for Ebola is currently available, promising results have been observed in experimental therapies. Antisense prevention therapies targeting the Ebola virus have shown efficacy in monkey studies. Administration of a coagulation inhibitor (rNAPc2) has also demonstrated some benefit in animal models. However, results from post-exposure vaccination, passive immunization with blood or serum, or recombinant human monoclonal antibodies in human survivors remain inconclusive.
